# Deuteronomy Chapter 5 — SOPHIA Consensus Translation
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **Sources:** EMET (Literal), LOGOS (Formal), PNEUMA (Dynamic)
**Hebrew Base:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 202–203
**LXX Reference:** Codex Vaticanus (Vat.gr.1209), pp. 147–148
**Disagreement Log:** `disagreements/DEU_005.md`

---

## Council Notes

Chapter 5 is the second giving of the Decalogue — not a repetition but a recontextualization. Moses addresses the new generation standing in Moab and claims, with striking boldness, that the covenant at Horeb was made with *them* (vv.2–3), not merely with the ancestors who died in the wilderness. The Decalogue here differs from Exodus 20 in several significant ways: (1) the Sabbath commandment is grounded in the Exodus from slavery rather than in creation; (2) the coveting commandment uses two distinct verbs (*lo tachmod* for the wife, *lo tit'aveh* for the house and property); (3) the wife is listed before the house and field; (4) several commandments are accompanied by the clause "as the LORD your God commanded you." These textual differences are preserved without harmonization.

Translator agreement was strong on the framing verses (vv.1–5, 22–33) and on the short apodictic commandments (vv.17–19). The most significant disagreements fell on: the rendering of *shav'* in vv.11 and 20 (LOGOS inserted "destructive," which SOPHIA rejects as an interpretive addition); the Shabbat opening verb (*shamor* — "keep" vs. "observe"); the description of God in v.9 (*El qanna* — "jealous God" maintained); the rendering of the ten-thousandfold grace in v.10; and the divine lament in v.29. PNEUMA's dynamic expansions at vv.9, 10, 22, 28, and 29 were noted; several were adopted where they clarified without altering. LOGOS's added gloss "and destructive" in v.11 was rejected; EMET's stark literalism at v.29 ("O that there were in their heart such a heart as this") was preferred over both alternatives for its rhetorical force.

Key rulings for this chapter: *shav'* = "emptiness" (not "vain" or "vain and destructive"); *shamor* = "keep" (not "observe"); *qanna* = "jealous"; *Ed shav'* (v.20) = "false witness" (following the LXX's practical rendering over etymological literalism); the two-verb structure of v.21 preserved (*covet* / *desire*); "O that" for the divine optative in v.29 (EMET); "son of Israel" place-name forms in English (standard project convention).

The LXX at v.20 reads *martys pseudēs* ("false witness"), harmonizing toward Exodus's *shaqer* rather than preserving Deuteronomy's *shav'*. SOPHIA follows the MT distinction but renders it into English as "a lying witness" to serve clarity while acknowledging the textual difference in the notes.

---

## Consensus Translation

1 And Moses summoned all Israel and said to them: "Hear, O Israel, the statutes and the ordinances that I am speaking in your ears today, and you shall learn them and take care to do them.

2 The LORD our God made a covenant with us at Horeb.

3 Not with our fathers did the LORD make this covenant, but with us — we, all of us who are alive here today.

4 Face to face the LORD spoke with you at the mountain from the midst of the fire —

5 I was standing between the LORD and you at that time to declare to you the word of the LORD, for you were afraid of the fire and did not go up the mountain — saying:

6 'I am the LORD your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.

7 You shall have no other gods before me.

8 You shall not make for yourself a carved image — any likeness of what is in the heavens above, or what is on the earth below, or what is in the waters below the earth.

9 You shall not bow down to them or serve them, for I, the LORD your God, am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, upon the third and upon the fourth generation of those who hate me,

10 but showing covenant-faithfulness to thousands — to those who love me and keep my commandments.

11 You shall not lift up the name of the LORD your God to emptiness, for the LORD will not hold guiltless the one who lifts up his name to emptiness.

12 Keep the Sabbath day to sanctify it, as the LORD your God commanded you.

13 Six days you shall labor and do all your work,

14 but the seventh day is a Sabbath to the LORD your God. You shall not do any work — you, or your son or your daughter, or your male servant or your female servant, or your ox or your donkey or any of your livestock, or the sojourner who is within your gates — so that your male servant and your female servant may rest as you do.

15 And you shall remember that you were a slave in the land of Egypt, and the LORD your God brought you out from there with a strong hand and an outstretched arm. Therefore the LORD your God commanded you to keep the Sabbath day.

16 Honor your father and your mother, as the LORD your God commanded you, so that your days may be long and that it may go well with you in the land that the LORD your God is giving you.

17 You shall not murder.

18 And you shall not commit adultery.

19 And you shall not steal.

20 And you shall not testify against your neighbor as a lying witness.

21 And you shall not covet your neighbor's wife. And you shall not desire your neighbor's house, his field, or his male servant or his female servant, his ox or his donkey, or anything that belongs to your neighbor.

22 These words the LORD spoke to your entire assembly at the mountain from the midst of the fire, the cloud, and the thick darkness — a great voice — and he added nothing more. And he wrote them on two tablets of stone and gave them to me.

23 And it came to pass, when you heard the voice from the midst of the darkness while the mountain was burning with fire, that you drew near to me — all the heads of your tribes and your elders —

24 and you said: "Behold, the LORD our God has shown us his glory and his greatness, and we have heard his voice from the midst of the fire. This day we have seen that God speaks with man and man still lives.

25 And now, why should we die? For this great fire will consume us. If we go on hearing the voice of the LORD our God any more, we shall die.

26 For who is there of all flesh who has heard the voice of the living God speaking from the midst of the fire, as we have, and lived?

27 You go near and hear all that the LORD our God will say, and you speak to us all that the LORD our God speaks to you, and we will hear and do it."

28 And the LORD heard the voice of your words when you spoke to me, and the LORD said to me: "I have heard the voice of the words of this people that they have spoken to you. They have spoken well in all that they have said.

29 O that there were in them such a heart as this — to fear me and to keep all my commandments always — so that it might go well with them and with their children forever!

30 Go, say to them: Return to your tents.

31 But you — stand here with me, and I will speak to you all the commandments and the statutes and the ordinances that you shall teach them, and they shall do them in the land that I am giving them to possess.'

32 And you shall take care to do as the LORD your God commanded you; you shall not turn aside to the right or to the left.

33 In all the way that the LORD your God has commanded you, you shall walk, so that you may live and it may go well with you, and you may prolong your days in the land that you are to possess.

---

## Verse-by-Verse Ruling Notes

**V.1 — "called" vs. "summoned":** EMET: "called to all Yisra'el." LOGOS: "summoned all Israel." PNEUMA: "Moses summoned all Israel." The Hebrew *vayiqra* = "and he called." SOPHIA: "summoned" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) — Moses is calling an assembly; "summoned" carries appropriate formality for this setting.

**V.1 — "ordinances" vs. "judgments":** EMET/PNEUMA: "ordinances." LOGOS: "judgments." SOPHIA: "ordinances" — consistent ruling with Deuteronomy 4 and throughout the project.

**V.2 — "cut a covenant" vs. "made a covenant":** EMET: "cut with us a covenant." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "made a covenant with us." The Hebrew *karat berit* = "cut a covenant" — the idiom of covenant-cutting. SOPHIA: "made a covenant" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) — "cut" is accurate and preserves the ritual etymology, but in running English narrative "made" is the established and natural rendering without loss of meaning; the textual note preserves the underlying idiom.

**V.5 — "because of" vs. "of" the fire:** EMET: "for you were afraid of the fire." LOGOS: "for you were afraid because of the fire." PNEUMA: "because you were afraid of the fire." SOPHIA: "for you were afraid of the fire" (EMET) — terse and accurate; "because of" adds a preposition not in the Hebrew.

**V.6 — "house of slaves" vs. "house of slavery":** EMET: "house of slaves." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "house of slavery." The Hebrew *beit avadim* = "house of slaves/slavery." SOPHIA: "house of slavery" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) — the Deuteronomic idiom refers to the social condition, not literally a house owned by slaves. Consistent with Deut 4.

**V.8 — "carved image" rendering:** EMET: "carved image — any form." LOGOS: "carved image — any likeness." PNEUMA: "idol — any carved image." SOPHIA: "carved image — any likeness" (LOGOS). The Hebrew *pesel* (carved image) followed by *temunah* (form/likeness). PNEUMA's restructuring ("idol — any carved image") inverts the terms; EMET's "form" is accurate but "likeness" is more standard for *temunah*.

**V.9 — "sons" vs. "children" for *banim*:** EMET: "upon sons." LOGOS: "upon the children." PNEUMA: "on the children." The Hebrew *banim* can mean sons or children. SOPHIA: "upon the children" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) — the generational curse operates on offspring generally, not restricted by gender.

**V.9 — "those who hate me" vs. "those who reject me":** EMET/LOGOS: "those who hate me." PNEUMA: "those who reject me." Hebrew *sone'ay* = participle of *sane'* — to hate. SOPHIA: "those who hate me" (EMET/LOGOS) — the Hebrew is precise; *sane'* means hate, not reject.

**V.10 — "to thousands" vs. "to the thousandth generation":** EMET: "to thousands." LOGOS: "to thousands of those who love me." PNEUMA: "to the thousandth generation." The Hebrew *la-alaphim* = "to thousands" (a collective plural, not specifying generations). SOPHIA: "to thousands" (EMET base) with LOGOS's relative clause — the Hebrew does not say "thousandth generation"; PNEUMA's expansion, while theologically apt, goes beyond the MT.

**V.11 — *shav'* rendering — "emptiness" vs. "in vain" vs. "in a vain and destructive way":** EMET: "to emptiness." LOGOS: "in a vain and destructive way." PNEUMA: "misuse." The Hebrew *la-shav'* = to emptiness/vanity/nothingness. SOPHIA: "to emptiness" (EMET) — "in vain" is too idiomatic; LOGOS's addition of "destructive" imports a connotation not present in *shav'*; PNEUMA's "misuse" is too imprecise.

**V.12 — *shamor* — "Keep" vs. "Observe":** EMET: "Keep the Shabbat day." LOGOS: "Observe the Sabbath day." PNEUMA: "Keep the Sabbath day." The Hebrew *shamor* = to keep, guard, observe. SOPHIA: "Keep" (EMET/PNEUMA) — Deuteronomy's *shamor* (keep/guard) distinguishes this account from Exodus 20's *zakhor* (remember). "Observe" (LOGOS) is also accurate but less common as a rendering for *shamor*; "keep" is the dominant English form and more naturally paired with "commandments/statutes" elsewhere.

**V.12 — "Shabbat" vs. "Sabbath":** EMET: "Shabbat." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "Sabbath." SOPHIA: "Sabbath" (LOGOS/PNEUMA) — English form consistent with project convention for proper nouns.

**V.14 — "male servant / female servant" vs. "male slave / female slave":** EMET: "male servant / female servant." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "male slave / female slave." The Hebrew *eved / amah* can mean either servant or slave. SOPHIA: "male servant / female servant" (EMET) — consistent with established project convention. "Slave" is accurate but the project uses "servant" for *eved* in household contexts throughout.

**V.14 — "as you do" vs. "as you rest" vs. "as [you rest]":** EMET: "may rest as [you rest]." LOGOS: "may rest as well as you." PNEUMA: "may rest just as you do." The Hebrew *kamokha* = "like you." SOPHIA: "may rest as you do" — natural English, accurate, without LOGOS's added "as well as" which adds a concessive nuance not in *kamokha*.

**V.15 — "a strong hand" vs. "a mighty hand":** EMET: "with a strong hand." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "with a mighty hand." Hebrew *yad chazaqah* = strong/firm hand. SOPHIA: "a strong hand" (EMET) — consistent ruling throughout Deuteronomy; *chazaq* = strong (not *gibor* = mighty).

**V.15 — "to keep the Sabbath day" vs. "to do the Sabbath day":** EMET: "to do the Shabbat day." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "to keep the Sabbath day." Hebrew *la'asot et-yom ha-Shabbat* — literally "to do/make the Sabbath day," but in English "keep" is the established idiom for observing a day. SOPHIA: "to keep the Sabbath day" (LOGOS/PNEUMA).

**V.16 — "so that your days may be long" vs. "so that you may live long":** EMET: "so that your days may be lengthened." LOGOS: "so that your days may be long." PNEUMA: "so that you will live long." Hebrew *le-ma'an ya'arikun yamekha* = so that your days may be lengthened. SOPHIA: "so that your days may be long" (LOGOS) — natural English equivalent of the lengthening idiom.

**V.20 — *ed shav'* — "false witness" vs. "witness of falsehood" vs. "lying witness":** EMET: "a witness of falsehood." LOGOS: "a false witness." PNEUMA: "false testimony." Hebrew *ed shav'* = a witness of *shav'* (emptiness/falsehood). SOPHIA: "a lying witness" — preserves the witness-as-person formulation (against PNEUMA's shift to "testimony") while rendering *shav'* with functional clarity. "False witness" (LOGOS) is also acceptable; "a lying witness" is slightly sharper in English.

**V.21 — "covet" vs. "desire" for the two verbs:** EMET: "You shall not covet...you shall not desire." LOGOS: "You shall not covet...you shall not desire." PNEUMA: "You shall not covet...You shall not crave." Hebrew *lo tachmod* (covet) for wife / *lo tit'aveh* (desire/crave) for house and property. SOPHIA: "covet...desire" (EMET/LOGOS) — the two-verb distinction must be preserved; "crave" (PNEUMA) for *tit'aveh* is accurate but less precise in the distinction from *chamad*.

**V.22 — "he added nothing more" vs. "he added not":** EMET: "a great voice and he added not [to it]." LOGOS: "a great voice — and he added nothing more." PNEUMA: "He added nothing more." SOPHIA: "a great voice — and he added nothing more" (LOGOS) — the bracketed addition in EMET is unnecessary; PNEUMA's period breaks off the participial flow.

**V.22 — "entire assembly" vs. "all your assembly":** EMET: "to all your assembly." LOGOS: "to your entire assembly." PNEUMA: "to your whole assembly." SOPHIA: "to your entire assembly" (LOGOS) — "entire" better conveys *kol* in this context of a formal assembly.

**V.24 — "man still lives" vs. "he lives":** EMET: "God speaks with man and he lives." LOGOS: "God speaks with man and man still lives." PNEUMA: "God can speak with a person and the person still lives." SOPHIA: "God speaks with man and man still lives" (LOGOS) — the reflexive repetition of "man" (singular subject carried through) is more natural than EMET's ambiguous pronoun; PNEUMA's "can speak" adds a modal that softens the declarative force.

**V.25 — "if we go on hearing" vs. "if we continue hearing" vs. "if we hear any more":** EMET: "if we continue hearing." LOGOS/PNEUMA: "if we hear...any more." SOPHIA: "if we go on hearing...any more" — a hybrid that captures the continuative aspect of *le-hosif* (to continue/add to).

**V.28 — "They have done well" vs. "They have spoken well" vs. "Everything they said is good":** EMET: "They have done well in all that they have spoken." LOGOS: "All that they have spoken is good." PNEUMA: "Everything they said is good." Hebrew *hetivo kol asher diberu* = "they have done well / it is good — all that they have spoken." SOPHIA: "They have spoken well in all that they have said" (EMET restructured) — preserves the verbal commendation (*hetivo* = they have done/acted well) over LOGOS's nominalization.

**V.29 — divine optative — "O that" vs. "Oh that" vs. "If only":** EMET: "O that there were in their heart such a heart as this." LOGOS: "Oh, that their heart were like this." PNEUMA: "If only their hearts would be inclined to fear me." SOPHIA: "O that there were in them such a heart as this" (EMET-based) — the literal Hebrew *mi-yitten ve-hayah levavam zeh lahem* ("who will give that this heart were in them") is an optative of divine wishing. EMET's rendering preserves this rhetorical register most faithfully; PNEUMA's "inclined" adds a word not in the MT.

**V.31 — "commandments and the statutes and the ordinances" vs. "commandments and the statutes and the judgments":** EMET: "the commandment and the statutes and the ordinances." LOGOS: "the commandments and the statutes and the judgments." PNEUMA: "the commandments, statutes, and ordinances." SOPHIA: "the commandments and the statutes and the ordinances" — consistent with "ordinances" for *mishpatim* throughout; EMET's singular "commandment" (*ha-mitsvah*) for the collective is grammatically accurate but the plural is clearer in English.

**V.33 — "prolong your days" vs. "lengthen days":** EMET: "you may lengthen days." LOGOS: "prolong your days." PNEUMA: "you will live long." SOPHIA: "prolong your days" (LOGOS) — idiomatic English equivalent of the Hebrew *ha'arakht yamim*. PNEUMA's "live long" loses the "days" image.

---

## Textual Notes for the Consensus Record

**Vv.2–3 — Covenant contemporaneity:** Moses' claim that the covenant was made "not with our fathers but with us" is a theological declaration that every generation of Israel stands before Sinai. The "fathers" here are the Exodus generation who perished in the wilderness — they are the immediate ancestors, not the patriarchs. This is one of Deuteronomy's most characteristic theological moves.

**V.4–5 — The face-to-face paradox:** Moses asserts that God spoke "face to face" with Israel at the mountain (v.4), then immediately qualifies that he himself stood as mediator (v.5). The tension is unresolved in the text. The paradox is integral to Deuteronomy's theology of word: Israel experienced the divine presence through the spoken word, even though Moses was its vehicle.

**V.12 — *Shamor* vs. *Zakhor*:** Deuteronomy 5:12 uses *shamor* (keep/guard); Exodus 20:8 uses *zakhor* (remember). The rabbinic tradition held that both were spoken simultaneously (*dibur echad*). SOPHIA preserves the distinction by translating each according to its own text.

**V.15 — Sabbath grounded in Exodus, not creation:** Deuteronomy's reason for the Sabbath is humanitarian-theological: "you were a slave in Egypt." Exodus 20:11 grounds it in creation rest (imitatio Dei). Both rationales are theologically coherent and complementary; SOPHIA follows each text as it stands without harmonization.

**Vv.17–21 — The apodictic commandments:** The sixth through tenth commandments are given in the shortest Hebrew formulations (two or three words each in Hebrew). Their terseness is part of their rhetorical power. SOPHIA maintains the short declarative form throughout.

**V.20 — *Shav'* vs. *Shaqer*:** Deuteronomy uses *shav'* (emptiness/vanity) for the false witness; Exodus 20:16 uses *shaqer* (lie/falsehood). The terms overlap but are not identical. *Shav'* has broader semantic range — it can include technically true but misleading testimony. SOPHIA renders "a lying witness" as a functional equivalent that preserves the personal witness formulation.

**V.21 — Two-verb coveting commandment:** Deuteronomy uses *lo tachmod* (do not covet) for the neighbor's wife and *lo tit'aveh* (do not desire) for the house, field, and property. Exodus 20:17 uses only *lo tachmod* for the entire prohibition, and places the house before the wife. The Deuteronomic version may reflect the beginning of a legal tradition distinguishing between the wrongful desire of a person and the wrongful desire of property.

**V.22 — *Ve-lo yasaf* ("and he added not"):** This phrase is one of the most debated in the Decalogue. It likely means the Ten Words constitute the complete divine speech at Horeb — nothing was added to them. The LXX preserves *kai ou prosethēken* exactly.
